strengths: Addresses critical gap: First comprehensive benchmark for long-prompt T2I evaluation with prompts averaging 284.89 tokens, significantly longer than prior work (DensePrompts ~100, DPG-Bench ~84)

Excellent data quality validation: Human evaluation confirms 93-100% quality across task-specific metrics; two-stage construction with model refinement; multi-faceted extraction pipeline with auxiliary techniques

Robust evaluation methodology: Cross-evaluator consistency verified with alternative MLLM (Kendall's Tau 0.88-1.0, Appendix I); randomness analysis showing negligible variations (<0.5%, Appendix J); thorough ablation studies on auxiliary techniques
Comprehensive annotation scale: 4,116 prompts with 37,165 character attributes, 6,910 location annotations, 18,526 relationship annotations enabling fine-grained compositional analysis

Valuable empirical insights: Clear metric difficulty hierarchy; demonstrates long-prompt training matters more than expanded context windows; negative correlation between prompt length and accuracy holds even for detected characters (Appendix N)

Strong reproducibility: Detailed implementation (Appendix E LLM prompts, C configs, D resources); mini-benchmark variant for resource-constrained evaluation (Appendix L); comprehensive statistical analysis
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on single MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct) for both data construction and evaluation despite mitigation efforts; alternative evaluator (InternVL3-9B) shows score inflation, indicating absolute scores may be evaluator-dependent
Coarse-grained evaluation metrics: Binary yes/no MLLM judgments lack nuance; cannot capture fine-grained alignment errors or partial correctness
Limited methodological novelty: Data construction follows established patterns (detailed captions → LLM extraction); evaluation dimensions are predictable extensions of T2I-CompBench and DPG-Bench

Somewhat predictable findings: SOTA models outperforming baselines, longer prompts being harder, and specialized training helping are intuitive; limited actionable insights for practitioners on solving identified problems

Dataset scope limitations: Filtering for ≥4 main characters may bias toward complex scenes; scene attributes achieve ~95% accuracy suggesting ceiling effects; derives from limited source datasets (DOCCI, Localized Narratives)
Spatial partitioning design choices lack sensitivity analysis: 75% coverage threshold and overlapping region boundaries appear somewhat arbitrary despite validation

Complex pipeline reproducibility: Multi-stage construction with numerous auxiliary tools and specific model versions may be challenging to reproduce exactly; potential for error accumulation across stages

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in long-prompt T2I evaluation with substantial scale (4,116 prompts, 284.89 avg tokens—3× larger than DPG-Bench)
Comprehensive evaluation across 12 models with clear findings on prompt length degradation and importance of long-prompt training over just expanded token capacity
Detailed attribute extraction pipeline combining MLLMs with auxiliary tools (object detectors, BLIP) to ground outputs in visual features
Provides mini-benchmark variant (800 samples) for accessibility and extensive supplementary materials including human evaluation, robustness analysis, and case studies
Clear practical motivation and potential community impact through open-source release (promised)
weaknesses: Critical circularity in pipeline: attributes extracted by LLMs → incorporated into prompts by LLMs → evaluated by LLMs. While Appendix I re-evaluates with InternVL, this only confirms relative rankings are consistent, not that metrics validly measure T2I capability. Missing human correlation studies of MLLM-based evaluation rankings.

Evaluation metrics rely on subjective binary yes/no MLLM judgments without calibration or validation. No analysis of how MLLM strictness compares to human judgment for 'attribute presence,' 'spatial alignment,' or 'scene coherence.' Entity Relationship evaluation has only 88.58% human agreement.

Limited novelty: attribute extraction uses standard MLLM prompting; evaluation dimensions (attributes, locations, scene properties) are known from prior work (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench). Core contribution is scale/aggregation, not methodology—insufficient for a top-tier venue.

Experimental confounds undermine comparisons: different resolutions (512×512 vs. 1024×1024), varying guidance scales/inference steps; admitted inability to test optimized methods on their intended backbones (superior versions unavailable open-source). No controlled ablations isolating long-prompt training effects.

Shallow root cause analysis: identifies error patterns (real-world priors, complex descriptions, cascading failures) but hypotheses about 'flattened compositional grammar' and 'attribute leakage' are stated without empirical validation. No ablations on architecture, data, or tokenizer effects.

Data quality concerns: LLM-based attribute extraction introduces bias toward LLM-interpretable features; filtering unincorporated attributes creates selection bias; 6.4% hallucination rate; no analysis of domain/category distribution or representativeness of real user prompts.

Incomplete benchmark analysis: no direct evaluation on existing benchmarks (DensePrompts, DPG-Bench) with same models; Scene Attributes substantially easier (50% hard samples vs. 80%+ for Locations), suggesting imbalanced difficulty; no cross-benchmark consistency analysis.

Reproducibility constraints: code/data unavailable during review; computational requirements high (10 GPU-hours per full evaluation, 20GB+ VRAM); MLLM/LLM selection (Qwen) critical but reproducibility depends on exact versions. Human evaluation limited to 400/4116 samples (9.7%) with no inter-annotator agreement reported.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark addressing a genuine gap: First large-scale dedicated benchmark (4,116 prompts, avg. 284.89 tokens) for evaluating long-prompt T2I generation, significantly exceeding prior work in scope and detail

Rigorous multi-stage benchmark construction with extensive validation: Systematic attribute extraction pipeline with dual-model verification, human evaluation (93.6% visual fidelity, 97.5% prompt consistency), and iterative refinement showing high-quality data

Exceptional robustness and transparency: Cross-evaluator validation preserving model rankings (Kendall's Tau 0.879-1.0), randomness analysis (<0.5% variation), LLM bias mitigation via auxiliary techniques (16.6% coordinate correction, 15.1% attribute gain from cropping), mini-benchmark for resource-constrained evaluation

Actionable empirical insights with clear practical implications: Long-prompt training matters more than token capacity (ParaDiffusion vs. LLM4GEN); metric difficulty hierarchy established (Character Locations most challenging); consistent prompt length degradation across models; architectural bottlenecks limit long-prompt optimized methods

Comprehensive four-dimensional evaluation framework strategically targeting key failure modes: Character Attributes, Locations, Scene Attributes, and Relationships; fine-grained category-specific analysis (objects/animals/persons); dual-model verification for character detection

High practical value and reproducibility: Open-sourcing dataset, data curation code, evaluation tools, and Data-Juicer integration; resource consumption documented; detailed LLM prompts provided; honest limitations discussion

Thorough evaluation across diverse model landscape: 7 general-purpose models (including SOTA FLUX, GPT Image-1) plus 5 long-prompt optimized methods; demonstrates consistent limitations across architectures
weaknesses: Fundamental reliance on MLLM-based evaluation introduces systematic biases: While cross-evaluator validation provided, InternVL3-9B shows ~10-15% score inflation and higher 'yes' bias; circular dependency between data construction and evaluation using Qwen models (mitigated but not eliminated); computational overhead (20GB+ VRAM, 10 hours) limits accessibility

Limited data source diversity potentially introducing dataset bias: All prompts from only 3 sources (DOCCI, Flickr30k, COCO); style degradation in optimized models (67.45% vs. 83.65% for lighting/style) suggests realistic-style bias; limited exploration of inherent source biases

Shallow failure mode analysis lacking causal investigation: Hypotheses about 'encoder flattening' and 'diffusion attribute leakage' are speculative without direct validation; no investigation of whether failures stem from text encoding vs. cross-attention vs. generation; suggested solutions are directional but untested

Limited statistical rigor in empirical analysis: No confidence intervals on reported accuracies; no significance testing between models; correlation analysis (Figure 3) lacks formal regression with p-values; mini-benchmark score differences explained informally without statistical validation; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for human evaluation

Human evaluation covers only 1.3% of data (400 of 4,116 samples): 50 samples per dimension insufficient for comprehensive validation; no formal reliability testing (Cronbach's alpha, ICC); some anomalous scores (100% Categorical Verification but 88.58% alignment) suggesting inconsistency; evaluator expertise not described

Cascading evaluation dependencies limit error source isolation: Character omission errors propagate to downstream metrics; unclear how much Entity Relationship failures stem from character detection vs. true relationship reasoning; sequential evaluation makes disentangling failure causes difficult

Potential prompt engineering effects not fully explored: Iterative LLM refinement using category-specific templates may implicitly favor LLM-based text encoders (T5, Llama); no ablation on prompt formulation impact; risk of optimizing benchmark to specific architecture families

Limited coverage of long-prompt specialized models: Only 5 optimized models evaluated; most use older backbones (SD1.5/SD-XL) due to availability; can't assess potential of modern architectures with dedicated training; proprietary models evaluated via API with uncontrolled inference details

Methodological novelty limited to systematic benchmark construction: Data pipeline competently combines existing techniques (MLLMs, detectors, LLM extraction) with no fundamentally new components; evaluation metrics follow standard cross-modal assessment approaches; contribution primarily in execution rather than innovation

Evaluation dimension scope may not exhaustively capture long-prompt adherence: Scene Attributes evaluated only at image level, not spatially granular; Entity Relationships limited to spatial/interactive, missing semantic relationships; text rendering fidelity not assessed; object count accuracy not included

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: comprehensive benchmark for long-prompt T2I generation with 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens, significantly longer than prior work

Rigorous evaluation methodology: 19 models across 5 paradigms, extensive robustness checks (cross-evaluator validation, model size variants, random seed analysis, bias mitigation studies), human evaluation showing 93.6% constraint grounding correctness

Well-designed benchmark structure: four evaluation dimensions systematically targeting identified challenges, grounded in real image-caption pairs rather than synthetic prompts, fine-grained annotation pipeline with multiple validation stages

Valuable empirical insights: clear negative correlation between prompt length and adherence, demonstrates long-prompt training matters more than expanded context windows, characterizes 'attribute leakage' phenomenon, identifies performance hierarchy across tasks

Strong reproducibility support: extensive appendix (36 pages) with detailed implementations, open-sourced resources promised, mini-benchmark for resource-constrained evaluation, lightweight evaluator option, good documentation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: contribution is primarily benchmarking rather than methodology; data pipeline uses existing techniques (MLLM extraction, YOLO detection); no new training methods or architectural insights proposed, reducing scientific impact

MLLM-based evaluation structural bias: using Qwen2.5-VL for both data construction and evaluation creates inherent bias; while robustness checks provided, InternVL3-9B evaluation shows 20-30% score inflation; no ground truth comparison; binary yes/no judgments miss nuanced partial correctness

Dataset construction opacity: rationale for two-round processing unclear; 8.5% filtering rate after first round lacks transparent analysis; MLLM sensitivity high (InternVL reduces attributes by 24.5%) but not thoroughly investigated; character filtering (>4 required) introduces distribution bias

Shallow mechanistic analysis of failures: 'attribute leakage' identified but not explained mechanistically; error analysis cites 'visual prior conflicts' without investigating architectural causes; why advanced models still fail at spatial reasoning unexplored; limited taxonomy of failure modes

Narrow experimental scope: 2×2 ablation only on SD-XL with added T5, pattern not validated across autoregressive/unified architectures; Qwen-Image success not deeply analyzed; limited short-prompt validation (single benchmark); missing ablations on individual dimension contributions

Unvalidated professional use case: claims to target professional applications but doesn't validate tasks reflect real workflows; domain bias toward spatial-relationship-poor images (93.26% missing locations); no evidence benchmark difficulty matches professional needs

Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals or significance tests between models; Nano Banana 2 deviates from SOTA trends suggesting possible artifacts; sample size imbalance across categories; correlation coefficients not consistently reported

Sensitivity analysis gaps: spatial partitioning 75% threshold not justified; IoU≥0.7 character matching thresholds not analyzed; 'perfect match' attribute criterion subjective; reproducibility depends on LLM prompt wording across 7-stage pipeline

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: evaluating T2I models on long, detail-rich prompts with clear practical motivation
Comprehensive benchmark construction grounded in real images with multi-stage validation (4,116 prompts, 284.89 avg tokens, substantially longer than prior work)
Extensive robustness validation including cross-evaluator consistency, evaluator size ablations, seed robustness analysis, and human evaluation (93.6% grounding correctness)
Broad empirical coverage across 19 models spanning 5 paradigms with clear performance hierarchies established
Valuable finding from ablation that long-prompt training matters more than expanded context windows alone
Excellent reproducibility documentation with detailed methodology and promised open-sourcing
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily a benchmark paper using standard techniques (MLLM extraction, object detection, spatial partitioning) with no novel methods, architectures, or theoretical insights

Circular evaluation design: prompts augmented with LLM-extracted attributes then evaluated against those same attributes; 6.4% constraint-source image misalignment means partially evaluating against hallucinated features
Evaluation brittleness evidenced by extensive robustness checks required (multi-evaluator validation, small model variants, seed analysis) suggesting underlying fragility and MLLM-dependence

Shallow mechanistic analysis of failures: 'attribute leakage' identified but not rigorously characterized; error analysis mostly descriptive; proposed solutions (structure-aware prompts, object-centric models) speculative and unvalidated

Artificial benchmark design with acknowledged 'detail-overload scenarios' that may not reflect real-world applications; unclear if performance degradation with length reflects fundamental limitations or benchmark artificiality
Crude evaluation metrics: binary yes/no judgments for attributes, locations, and relationships with no partial credit, confidence intervals, or significance testing between models
No proposed solutions or methods: paper is diagnostic only, with limited actionable guidance for model developers beyond 'long-prompt training helps'
Statistical rigor issues: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or formal definitions (e.g., 'attribute leakage'); correlation analysis (Figure 3) lacks statistical validation
Limited practical guidance: unclear what 51% accuracy means for production applications; no discussion of acceptable performance thresholds or model fitness-for-purpose
Benchmark sustainability concerns: rapid model evolution evident from post-hoc addition of Nano Banana 2; without methodological contributions, benchmark may quickly become outdated

strengths: Important practical problem: Addresses genuine gap in long-prompt T2I evaluation for professional applications
Rigorous benchmark construction: 4,116 expert-validated prompts (avg. 284.89 tokens) grounded in real image-caption pairs with 93.6-100% quality metrics
Comprehensive evaluation design: Four complementary evaluation dimensions (attributes, locations, scene properties, relationships) targeting specific failure modes
Broad model coverage: 19 models spanning 5 paradigms (classical, flow-based, long-prompt optimized, MLLM-based, unified) capturing field evolution
Insightful analysis: Clear difficulty hierarchy, well-designed ablation study isolating training impact vs. context window, quantified prompt-length degradation
Extensive robustness validation: Cross-evaluator consistency checks, lightweight evaluator options, randomness analysis, mini-benchmark—all showing robustness
Reproducibility focus: Open-sourcing dataset/code, detailed methodology (26 appendix pages), LLM prompts, mini-benchmark for resource constraints
Well-presented: Clear figures, case studies, comprehensive supplementary materials without cluttering main text
weaknesses: MLLM-based evaluation dependency: Heavy reliance on single Qwen2.5-VL-7B for both data construction and evaluation introduces potential circular bias; cross-evaluator analysis shows score inflation with other MLLMs
Data construction artifacts: Final prompts intentionally diverge from source images (Entity Relationship-Image Alignment 88.58%); may artificially favor prompt-following over real-world fidelity
Binary evaluation metrics: Yes/no judgments don't capture partial correctness; coarse spatial discretization (9-region partitioning) may harshly penalize near-correct placements
Limited methodological novelty: Individual components (attribute extraction, LLM-based evaluation) use existing techniques; contribution is benchmark itself rather than new methods
Single ablation study: Token limit vs. training comparison only on modified SD-XL; generalization to other architectures (FLUX, etc.) unverified
Missing uncertainty quantification: No confidence intervals or statistical significance testing between model scores despite being core claims
Model reproducibility gaps: Some long-prompt optimized models lack optimal hyperparameters; proprietary models cannot be reproduced
Benchmark scope limitations: 4,116 prompts smaller than some general benchmarks; English-only; deliberately excludes aesthetic/safety dimensions
